stem:
A 4-month-old boy presents to the paediatric emergency department with 3 days of coryza, cough and increasing work of breathing. He is bottle-feeding at about 50 percent of normal intake and has had wet nappies overnight. He was born at 39 weeks by normal vaginal delivery with no neonatal issues and is fully immunised for age.

On arrival he has audible wheeze with mild subcostal recession. He accepts a small feed on your assessment and settles when held. His SpO2 on room air is 89 percent and stays at 89 to 90 percent when he is calm and awake.

data_table.Vital signs: Pulse 148/min, blood pressure not routinely measured, respiratory rate 52/min, SpO2 89 percent on room air, temperature 37.4 degrees C
data_table.Examination: Alert, pink centrally; mild subcostal recession; widespread expiratory wheeze and fine crackles; capillary refill under 2 seconds; anterior fontanelle flat
data_table.Investigations: No routine bloods or chest X-ray required

lead_in: What is the most appropriate initial oxygen strategy?

options.text: Give low-flow nasal prong oxygen at 1 to 2 L/min targeting SpO2 at or above 90 percent
options.rationale: RCH CPG uses low-flow nasal prong oxygen as first-line when SpO2 drops below 90 percent when awake, with 90 percent as the maintenance target. (Source: RCH CPG Bronchiolitis)

options.text: Withhold oxygen and observe overnight because he remains alert and feeding
options.rationale: Sustained awake SpO2 below 90 percent meets the RCH threshold for oxygen therapy irrespective of feeding. (Source: RCH CPG Bronchiolitis)

options.text: Trial nebulised salbutamol 2.5 mg once before considering any oxygen therapy
options.rationale: Bronchodilators are not recommended for infants under 12 months with typical bronchiolitis in the RCH pathway. (Source: RCH CPG Bronchiolitis)

options.text: Start CPAP via a paediatric interface at 6 cm H2O and admit to ICU immediately
options.rationale: CPAP or intubation follows escalation through low-flow then HFNC when respiratory failure develops; it is not first-line here. (Source: RCH CPG Bronchiolitis)

options.text: Start high-flow nasal cannula at 2 L/kg/min heated humidified oxygen now
options.rationale: HFNC is reserved for failure of low-flow oxygen after a trial of at least 1 to 2 hours; it is not the first oxygen escalation. (Source: RCH CPG Bronchiolitis)

explanation.summary: The RCH bronchiolitis pathway uses SpO2 of 90 percent as the maintenance target for infants over 6 weeks with typical bronchiolitis, and starts oxygen with low-flow nasal prongs at 1 to 2 L/min when SpO2 falls below 90 percent awake. HFNC is reserved for infants who fail low-flow after a 1 to 2 hour trial. Bronchodilators, steroids, adrenaline and antibiotics are not recommended in typical bronchiolitis. The pathway is one of supportive feeding, oxygenation and minimal handling.
key_points: SpO2 target on the RCH pathway is 90 percent, not 92 to 94 percent.
Low-flow nasal prongs 1 to 2 L/min are first-line oxygen.
HFNC follows failure of low-flow after 1 to 2 hours.
Bronchodilators and steroids are not recommended in bronchiolitis under 12 months.
explanation.pearls: On the RCH CPG start nasal prong oxygen at 1 to 2 L/min once SpO2 sits below 90 percent when the infant is calm and awake; only escalate to HFNC after 1 to 2 hours of failed low-flow.
